description: QVYX is a three-person student team from Tajikistan. Jahongir Norov, our captain, and Toir Turazoda develop the software; Zeboniso Azizova leads design, presentation, and the project submission. We brought these roles together to turn a space-health challenge into a working prototype with a real smartwatch and a web dashboard. Our different strengths help us test the same idea from the perspectives of the astronaut, the crew, and the person using the system.
summary: QVYX Health is a prototype that helps astronauts monitor their health and decide what to do when a reading changes. Smartwatches (on Wear OS) measure heart rate and send available readings directly to a server over Wi-Fi; the astronaut can see the current value and connection status on the watch and send a manual SOS. A web dashboard shows personal trends, manual health entries, crew status, and mission tasks. It compares heart rate with the astronaut’s own baseline and highlights deviations. Synthetic crew profiles demonstrate how the system works for a larger mission; they are clearly separate from real watch data. NASA DONKI solar-flare and solar-energetic-particle events add space-weather context. QVYX is a demonstration of astronaut self-assessment and crew support.
details:
How it works. The Wear OS app on a Galaxy Watch 4 displays measured heart rate and connection status. It sends telemetry to a FastAPI server over Wi‑Fi. The astronaut can press SOS on the watch; the crew dashboard receives the event with the current heart rate, or the last available reading when no fresh measurement exists. The web app shows trends against the astronaut’s personal baseline and allows manual entry of measurements the watch does not provide, including blood pressure, temperature, sleep, glucose, and physical activity.

Astronaut action. QVYX is designed to help the wearer interpret a change, not only to report it to Mission Control. The dashboard highlights a heart-rate deviation above 15% from the personal baseline. The astronaut can check the trend, repeat a measurement at rest, review their mission tasks, contact the crew medic when concerned, or send SOS from the watch. The watch can also display an alert sent by the server. The demo uses synthetic crew profiles to show these interactions alongside real watch telemetry; synthetic values are labelled as such.

NASA data. We use NASA’s DONKI space-weather service, specifically solar-flare (FLR) and solar-energetic-particle (SEP) event information, to provide context for possible radiation-related hazards. We combine this event information with NASA Human Research Program material on the hazards of spaceflight and reference information about altered gravity. DONKI events are not a measurement of an astronaut’s radiation dose; protective decisions require official mission alerts and dosimetry.
